title: Interpreters
why: An interpreter is the simplest complete language implementation: scanner, parser, AST, evaluator. Every compiler you build later reuses these front-end pieces, and a tree-walking interpreter is the reference semantics you test compiled code against.

steps.title: Crafting Interpreters ch. 2 A Map of the Territory
steps.detail: Read for the vocabulary (front end, IR, back end, tree-walk vs bytecode). Skip ch. 3 (Lox spec) on first pass; skim it as reference.

steps.title: Crafting Interpreters ch. 4 Scanning
steps.detail: Port jlox's scanner to Python and print the token stream for a few sample files. Do challenge 4 (C-style /* ... */ block comments, optionally nested).

steps.title: Crafting Interpreters ch. 5 Representing Code
steps.detail: Focus on the grammar notation and the Visitor pattern; in Python, dataclasses plus match statements replace the generated AST classes.

steps.title: Crafting Interpreters ch. 6 Parsing Expressions
steps.detail: Implement recursive descent with one function per precedence level and panic-mode synchronization (section 6.3). Print an S-expression for every parsed expression.

steps.title: Crafting Interpreters ch. 7 Evaluating Expressions
steps.detail: Write the evaluator with runtime type errors. This is your first working calculator REPL.

steps.title: Crafting Interpreters ch. 8 Statements and State
steps.detail: Add statements, globals, assignment and block scopes via an environment chain.

steps.title: Crafting Interpreters ch. 9 Control Flow and ch. 10 Functions
steps.detail: Add if/while/for (for desugars to while), then functions and closures (ch. 10). Ch. 10 adds the native clock() and a recursive fib example; keep it as your benchmark.

steps.title: Crafting Interpreters ch. 11 Resolving and Binding
steps.detail: Your first static pass over the AST: compute the scope distance of each variable use. Classes (ch. 12-13) are optional.

steps.title: Crafting Interpreters ch. 14 Chunks of Bytecode
steps.detail: Start Part III (clox, in C). Read ch. 14 and ch. 15 A Virtual Machine for the chunk format and the stack-based dispatch loop.

steps.title: Crafting Interpreters ch. 15-17: VM, Scanning on Demand, Compiling Expressions
steps.detail: Build the stack VM and the single-pass Pratt compiler in C. At the end of ch. 17 clox evaluates expressions only; functions arrive in ch. 24 Calls and Functions.

steps.title: Measure tree-walk vs bytecode
steps.detail: If you stopped at ch. 17, time both implementations on the same large generated arithmetic expression evaluated many times. If you reached ch. 24, time fib(30) in both. Record the numbers for the write-up.

build: A Python tree-walking interpreter for a Lox subset (expressions, variables, blocks, if/while/for, functions with closures) with a resolver pass, plus a C bytecode VM that evaluates arithmetic expressions through a Pratt compiler; include a test directory of .lox programs with expected outputs and a runner script.
check: Your parser reports an error on 'print (1 + ;' and continues parsing the next statement
Closures work: a makeCounter() function returns counters that increment independently
The resolver reports "Can't read local variable in its own initializer." for 'var a = a;' in a local scope
You have a timing table comparing your Python tree-walker and C clox on the same input

extra.title: Crafting Interpreters ch. 30 Optimization
extra.note: Profiling-driven changes to clox: faster hash table probing (30.2) and NaN boxing (30.3).

extra.title: Build Your Own Lisp
extra.note: Alternative C-based interpreter if you want more C practice.

effort: 30–45 h (14 chapters, about 2-3 h each including code)
outcomes: Write a scanner and a recursive-descent parser with precedence levels and panic-mode error recovery.
Implement lexical scoping, closures and a resolver pass in a tree-walking interpreter.
Explain, with a measured timing, why the clox bytecode VM is faster than the tree-walker.
stuck: Left recursion makes recursive descent call itself forever: rewrite the rule as a loop (section 6.2 Recursive Descent Parsing).
Closures capturing the wrong variable means names are being resolved dynamically; ch. 11 Resolving and Binding fixes exactly this bug.
Precedence bugs: print the S-expression of every parsed test case before evaluating it.
Skip full Lox parity (classes, inheritance) until expressions, statements, functions and closures pass your tests.

project.title: Bytecode VM for your Lox subset with a measured speedup
project.brief: Extend your tree-walking interpreter with a compiler to a stack-based bytecode and a dispatch-loop VM (in Python first, optionally C). Use the tree-walker as an oracle: a fuzzer generates random programs and asserts both produce identical output. Measure where the speedup comes from (dispatch, environment lookups vs local slots, constant folding at compile time).
deliverables: repo with scanner, parser, tree-walker, bytecode compiler, VM, and a differential fuzzer
README with a benchmark table (fib(25), loops, string concat) for tree-walk vs VM, plus a disassembler output example
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining the bytecode design, local-slot resolution, and what profiling showed about dispatch overhead

rubric.solid: VM passes every tree-walker test plus 1,000 fuzzed programs with zero divergences; at least 3x faster than the tree-walker on fib(25) in the same language.
rubric.exceptional: C VM with computed-goto dispatch, superinstructions justified by an opcode-pair frequency profile, 20x+ speedup, and a fuzzer bug found and documented.

references.title: Crafting Interpreters ch. 15 A Virtual Machine

title: Compiling to machine code
why: Turning an AST into real assembly shows what every ML compiler ultimately emits. Nora Sandler's incremental blog series plus the test suite for her book give a tight loop: one language feature at a time, each checked by a few dozen tests.

steps.title: x86 Assembly Guide (UVA CS216)
steps.detail: The guide covers 32-bit x86 registers and mov/push/pop/call/ret; the test suite needs x86-64, so also compile tiny C programs on Compiler Explorer with x86-64 gcc -O0 and read the output.

steps.title: Install the test suite and run --check-setup
steps.detail: Clone nlsandler/writing-a-c-compiler-tests and run './test_compiler --check-setup'. The suite follows the book's chapters, not the blog: it needs x86-64 (Rosetta on Apple Silicon), 'int main(void)', and the gcc-like driver plus --lex/--parse/--validate/--tacky/--codegen stage flags described in the README.

steps.title: Sandler Part 1: Integers -> run './test_compiler ./mycc --chapter 1'
steps.detail: Lexer, parser and code emission for 'int main(void){return 2;}'. The blog emits 32-bit x86; Part 1 itself recommends adapting to 64-bit, and the suite requires it. Use --latest-only while iterating, then rerun without it to catch regressions.

steps.title: Sandler Part 2: Unary Operators -> run './test_compiler ./mycc --chapter 2'
steps.detail: Add negation, bitwise complement and logical not. Each AST node maps to a short instruction template.

steps.title: Sandler Part 3: Binary Operators -> run './test_compiler ./mycc --chapter 3'
steps.detail: Add + - * /. The blog rewrites the grammar into exp/term/factor levels; the chapter 3 tests also include % (mod.c). Intermediate values live on the stack (push/pop).

steps.title: Sandler Part 4: Even More Binary Operators -> run './test_compiler ./mycc --chapter 4'
steps.detail: Add relational and short-circuiting && and ||, using labels and conditional jumps.

steps.title: Sandler Part 5: Local Variables -> run './test_compiler ./mycc --chapter 5'
steps.detail: Introduce stack frames, base-pointer-relative variable slots and a variable map; reject undeclared and redeclared variables.

steps.title: Sandler Part 6: Conditionals -> run './test_compiler ./mycc --chapter 6'
steps.detail: if statements and the ternary operator.

steps.title: Sandler Part 7: Compound Statements -> run './test_compiler ./mycc --chapter 7'
steps.detail: Block scoping and shadowing; free stack space when a scope closes.

steps.title: Sandler Part 8: Loops -> run './test_compiler ./mycc --chapter 8'
steps.detail: for, while and do loops plus break and continue; track the current loop's labels.

steps.title: Sandler Part 9: Functions -> run './test_compiler ./mycc --chapter 9'
steps.detail: The blog uses the 32-bit cdecl convention; implement the x86-64 System V convention instead (first six integer arguments in registers, 16-byte stack alignment at call). The chapter 9 tests include 'libraries' cases that link your code with gcc-compiled C.

steps.title: Sandler Part 10: Global Variables (optional; chapter 10 tests need static/extern)
steps.detail: File-scope variables in .data/.bss. The suite's chapter 10 tests also require static and extern, which the blog does not cover; treat chapter 10 as optional.

build: mycc: a Python C-subset compiler (int returns, unary/binary/relational/logical ops including %, locals, if/ternary, blocks, loops with break/continue, functions) emitting x86-64 assembly and passing './test_compiler ./mycc --chapter 9', plus a README mapping each blog part to commit hashes.
check: './test_compiler ./mycc --chapter 9' passes with zero failures
The chapter 9 'libraries' tests pass, so mycc functions link with gcc-compiled C in both directions
You can draw the stack frame of a call with 8 int arguments and say which arguments are in registers and which are on the stack
Invalid programs (undeclared variable, break outside a loop) exit nonzero and write no assembly file

extra.title: Writing a C Compiler (book, No Starch)
extra.note: The book adds a TACKY three-address IR from ch. 2, types in Part II, and TACKY optimizations and register allocation in Part III (ch. 19-20); the same test suite covers all of it. (nostarch.com blocks scripted fetches; check the TOC in a browser.)

extra.title: Compiler Explorer
extra.note: Compare your output to gcc -O0 and -O2 for each feature.

effort: 40–60 h (10 blog parts at 3-5 h each, plus porting from 32-bit to x86-64)
outcomes: Lower a C-subset AST to x86-64 assembly that assembles, links and runs.
Implement the System V x86-64 calling convention, including stack arguments and 16-byte alignment.
Use the book test suite's stage flags to localize a failure to the lexer, parser, validator or code generator.
stuck: Segfault on call: rsp must be 16-byte aligned at the call instruction (System V ABI).
Values clobbered after a call: caller-saved registers (rax, rcx, rdx, rsi, rdi, r8-r11) are not preserved.
Blog examples use int main() and 32-bit registers; the suite expects int main(void) and x86-64.
On Apple Silicon, run the suite and gcc under Rosetta ('arch -x86_64 zsh'); the runner refuses native arm64. Mach-O symbols need a leading underscore.

project.title: Three-address IR and peephole pass for mycc, measured against naive codegen
project.brief: Insert a TACKY-style three-address IR between the AST and assembly, give each temporary a stack slot, and add a peephole pass (drop push/pop pairs, redundant movs, jumps to the next label). Measure static instruction counts of the emitted assembly on the suite's chapter 1-9 valid programs before and after.
deliverables: repo with mycc, the IR stage, the peephole pass, and a script that counts emitted instructions per test program
README table: instructions per program for naive codegen, IR codegen, IR plus peephole, and gcc -O0
a 600–1200 word write-up on the IR design and which peephole rules paid off

rubric.solid: All chapter 1-9 tests still pass and total emitted instructions drop by at least 25% versus the naive stack codegen.
rubric.exceptional: Also passes with --bitwise --compound, and comes within 1.2x of gcc -O0 instruction count on the chapter 9 valid programs.

references.title: QBE compiler backend (a small reference backend)

title: IRs, SSA and optimization passes
why: Real compilers optimize on an intermediate representation, not the AST. CS6120 (Fall 2020, with a self-guided version) uses the Bril IR to teach control-flow graphs, dataflow analysis and SSA through small implementation tasks.

steps.title: CS6120 Lesson 1: Welcome & Overview
steps.detail: Read the lesson and the self-guided page (cs6120/2020fa/self-guided/), which explains how to do the course without enrollment.

steps.title: CS6120 Lesson 2: Representing Programs -- video + task
steps.detail: Install bril2json and brili. Do the task: write a Bril benchmark, and write a small tool that loads Bril JSON (for example, counts add instructions). Then form basic blocks and a CFG as the lesson derives.

steps.title: CS6120 Lesson 3: Local Analysis & Optimization -- video + task
steps.detail: Implement trivial dead code elimination (iterate to convergence) and local value numbering. Compare dynamic instruction counts with 'brili -p' on the benchmarks.

steps.title: CS6120 Lesson 4: Data Flow -- video + task
steps.detail: The task asks for at least one dataflow analysis; do the bonus generic worklist solver and instantiate it for reaching definitions and live variables.

steps.title: CS6120 Lesson 5: Global Analysis & SSA -- video + task part 1 (dominators)
steps.detail: Find dominators, build the dominator tree and compute dominance frontiers; test against brute-force path enumeration.

steps.title: CS6120 Lesson 5 task part 2: into and out of SSA
steps.detail: Implement into-SSA and out-of-SSA. Check SSA form with the lesson's is_ssa.py and run the midpoint under brili, which supports phi. Watch for variables undefined on some paths.

steps.title: CS6120 Lesson 6: LLVM -- video + task
steps.detail: The task: follow the LLVM for Grad Students tutorial far enough to write a pass that changes program execution (for example, print on every floating-point division). Requires C++ and an LLVM install; optional.

steps.title: CS6120 Lesson 7: Loop Optimization -- video + task
steps.detail: Implement natural loop detection and LICM on Bril (the lesson's recommended choice) and evaluate it on the Bril benchmarks.

steps.title: CS6120 Lesson 11: Dynamic Compilers
steps.detail: Watch the lecture. The task is a trace-based speculative optimizer for Bril: modify brili to record a trace and reinject it with the speculation extension. Lessons 8-10 are optional.

steps.title: Lower your Module 11 compiler through a Bril-like IR
steps.detail: Read the Bril language reference, then add a three-address IR stage to mycc from Module 11 and run your TDCE/LVN passes before codegen.

build: A Python optimizer for Bril with CFG construction, a worklist dataflow solver, dominators, into/out of SSA, TDCE+LVN and LICM; a script runs bril/benchmarks/core before and after and reports dynamic instruction counts from 'brili -p' with output checks.
check: Every program in bril/benchmarks/core prints the same output before and after your passes
LVN on 'a = add x y; b = add y x' reuses a (requires the commutativity extension)
is_ssa.py accepts your into-SSA output, and SSA round-trips give identical brili output
Your dominator tree for a hand-drawn nested-loop CFG matches a by-hand answer

extra.title: Engineering a Compiler (Cooper & Torczon) ch. 8-9
extra.note: 3rd edition: ch. 8 Introduction to Optimization, ch. 9 Data-Flow Analysis.

extra.title: SSA Book (Static Single Assignment Book)
extra.note: Free reference on SSA construction and destruction.

extra.title: Simple and Efficient Construction of SSA Form (Braun et al.)
extra.note: Alternative SSA construction used in many modern compilers.

effort: 40–55 h (6 lessons with tasks at 5-8 h each, plus the mycc IR stage)
outcomes: Build a CFG from Bril and convert it into and out of SSA using dominance frontiers.
Implement a worklist dataflow solver and instantiate it for at least two analyses.
Implement TDCE, LVN and LICM and measure their effect with dynamic instruction counts.
stuck: Phi placement errors usually come from a wrong dominator tree: test dominators alone on hand-drawn CFGs first.
Out-of-SSA with naive sequential copies hits the lost-copy and swap problems; the lesson links Boissinot et al. on correct translation.
A non-terminating dataflow solver means a transfer function that is not monotone (lesson 4 theory section).
Run each pass alone and check brili output against the unoptimized program before combining passes.

project.title: An optimizing middle-end with a measured pass pipeline
project.brief: Build an SSA middle-end on Bril with SCCP, GVN (the lesson 5 bonus), LICM and aggressive DCE, then study pass ordering. Report dynamic instruction counts from 'brili -p' on bril/benchmarks/core and check brili output equivalence after every pass.
deliverables: repo with IR, SSA construction/destruction, 4+ optimization passes and a pass manager
README with a table of dynamic instruction counts per benchmark per pass and a pass-ordering heatmap
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining SSA construction, why SCCP beats separate const-prop + DCE, and one miscompile you found

rubric.solid: All passes preserve output on every core benchmark; the full pipeline lowers dynamic instruction count on at least half the benchmarks and raises it on none.
rubric.exceptional: An exhaustive search over orders of the 4 passes with the best order per benchmark reported, and a random-program fuzzer that found and fixed at least one miscompile.

references.title: Simple and Efficient Construction of SSA Form (Braun et al.)

title: Term rewriting, e-graphs and lambda calculus
why: tinygrad's optimizer is a pattern-matching rewrite engine over a graph IR (UOps and PatternMatcher); e-graphs are the principled version of that idea. Lambda calculus gives you the formal vocabulary for substitution, binding and evaluation order that rewriting depends on.

steps.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Lambda Calculus, sections 1, 2 and 4
steps.detail: Section 2 covers syntax and free/bound variables; section 4 covers reduction and reduction strategies. Skip sections 5-9.

steps.title: Write a lambda calculus interpreter with capture-avoiding substitution
steps.detail: In Python, implement terms, capture-avoiding substitution and normal-order reduction; encode Church numerals and check that 2+3 reduces to 5.

steps.title: egg: Fast and Extensible Equality Saturation (POPL 2021 talk, 30 min)
steps.detail: Linked from the egg homepage. Watch for e-classes, rebuilding, equality saturation and extraction.

steps.title: egg paper: Fast and Extensible Equality Saturation
steps.detail: Read the introduction, background and rebuilding sections; skim the case studies. The intro's (a*2)/2 example shows why destructive rewriting depends on rule order.

steps.title: egg tutorials (Rust docs) or a Python reimplementation
steps.detail: The docs have three parts: background, getting started, explanations. Either follow them in Rust or write a tiny Python e-graph (union-find, hashcons, rebuild) for arithmetic.

steps.title: tinygrad docs: UOp
steps.detail: Read how tinygrad represents computation as UOp(op, src, arg) graphs. The pattern matcher is not documented there; read it in ops.py in the next step.

steps.title: Write a pattern-rewrite engine for an expression DAG
steps.detail: Read the UPat and PatternMatcher classes and graph_rewrite in this pinned ops.py, then write your own: patterns with wildcards, a fixed-point rewrite, and constant-folding and algebraic rules.

steps.title: Compare greedy rewriting vs equality saturation
steps.detail: Run the same rule set through your greedy rewriter and your e-graph on 10 expressions; record each case where greedy ends at a costlier result.

build: A Python rewrite toolkit with (1) a PatternMatcher-style greedy rewriter over a hash-consed expression DAG and (2) a mini e-graph with equality saturation and cost-based extraction, both applied to arithmetic/tensor-index expressions, with a report showing cases where saturation finds better results than greedy rewriting.
check: Substituting y into (\x.\y.x) renames the bound y, giving \y'.y
Church numeral 2+3 and 2*3 reduce to the normal forms of 5 and 6
Your e-graph proves (a*2)/2 == a with rules a*2->a<<1, (a*b)/c->a*(b/c), x/x->1, x*1->x, even though the shift rule also fires
Your greedy rewriter terminates on a rule set that contains a+b->b+a

extra.title: egglog
extra.note: egraphs + Datalog, from the same group as egg.

extra.title: Term Rewriting and All That (Baader & Nipkow)

effort: 25–40 h (lambda interpreter 4-6 h, egg talk and paper 4-6 h, e-graph 8-12 h, rewriter and comparison 8-12 h)
outcomes: Implement capture-avoiding substitution and normal-order reduction.
Build an e-graph with hashconsing, union-find, rebuilding and equality saturation, and extract terms with a cost function.
Explain where tinygrad's PatternMatcher and graph_rewrite get stuck that equality saturation does not.
stuck: Rewrites looping on a+b->b+a need a termination ordering or an e-graph instead of destructive rewriting.
E-graph blowup: set node and iteration limits; associativity plus commutativity together is the usual cause.
Wrong results after unions mean congruence was not restored; follow the egg paper's rebuilding section.
Substitution bugs are almost always variable capture: use de Bruijn indices or fresh names.

project.title: Equality-saturation optimizer for tensor expressions
project.brief: Build an e-graph optimizer for a small tensor algebra (matmul, add, transpose, elementwise ops) with 15+ rules such as transpose-of-transpose, (AB)^T = B^T A^T, matmul associativity and distributivity. Extract with a FLOP cost model and check it finds the optimal parenthesization for 10 matrix chains of length 4-6 (compare to the textbook O(n^3) dynamic program).
deliverables: repo with e-graph core (union-find, hashcons, rebuild), 15+ rules, and cost-based extraction
README with plots of e-graph size vs iterations and FLOP reductions on 10 test expressions, with numerical-equivalence checks in NumPy
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining equality saturation, rule explosion control, and extraction tradeoffs

rubric.solid: Matches the dynamic-programming optimal FLOP count on all 10 chains, NumPy results agree to 1e-6 relative error, and saturation stops cleanly at the node limit.
rubric.exceptional: ILP or tree-DP extraction compared with greedy extraction, the same rules run in egg for comparison, and random testing of every rule for soundness.

references.title: egg: Fast and extensible equality saturation

title: Automatic differentiation
why: ML compilers differentiate programs as a graph transformation. You build forward and reverse mode yourself, then read how JAX implements grad as linearize plus transpose on a traced IR (Autodidax).

steps.title: Karpathy: The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation: building micrograd
steps.detail: Code along to build micrograd's scalar Value class with backward().

steps.title: micrograd repo: reproduce engine.py and pass the tests
steps.detail: Re-implement engine.py from memory and check gradients against PyTorch as in test/test_engine.py.

steps.title: Autodiff Puzzles (Sasha Rush)
steps.detail: Solve all puzzles: derive and implement backward for each tensor op, checked numerically.

steps.title: Baydin et al., Automatic Differentiation in Machine Learning: a Survey
steps.detail: Read Section 2 (what AD is not) and Section 3 (forward mode with dual numbers, reverse mode). Skip Section 5, the survey of implementations.

steps.title: Implement forward mode with dual numbers
steps.detail: Add a Dual class supporting + * sin exp, compute JVPs, and compare costs with your reverse-mode for R^n->R vs R->R^n functions.

steps.title: Autodidax Part 1: Transformations as interpreters (standard evaluation, jvp, vmap)
steps.detail: Code along: primitives, the interpreter stack, and the JVP and vmap tracers.

steps.title: Autodidax Parts 2-3: Jaxprs and jit (simplified)
steps.detail: Continue through make_jaxpr and the simplified jit that lowers jaxprs to XLA. This is tracing a Python function into an IR.

steps.title: Autodidax Part 4: linearize and vjp (and grad)
steps.detail: Reverse mode as partial evaluation (linearize) followed by transposition. Implement grad in your mini system.

steps.title: Reverse-mode AD over your Module 13 DAG (read tinygrad mixin/gradient.py)
steps.detail: Read tinygrad's gradient.py (a rewrite-rule-based gradient), then emit gradient graphs for your own IR.

build: A Python tensor-free autodiff library with forward mode (dual numbers), reverse mode (tape/graph), and a tracing jit that records a jaxpr-like IR and computes grad as a transformation on that IR; validated against finite differences and PyTorch on 15 functions.
check: Gradients agree with central finite differences to 1e-5 on all test functions
You can explain why reverse mode costs O(1) passes for scalar loss and forward mode O(n)
Your traced IR for a 2-layer MLP prints readable and its grad IR runs correctly
Higher-order: grad(grad(f)) works for f=x**3

extra.title: The Simple Essence of Automatic Differentiation (Elliott)
extra.note: Category-theory view of AD as compositional.

outcomes: Implement reverse-mode AD on a graph with gradient accumulation for nodes used more than once.
Derive VJPs and JVPs for core ops and check them against central finite differences in float64.
State the cost of forward vs reverse mode for f: R^n -> R and f: R -> R^n.
Explain how Autodidax implements jvp, vmap, jit and vjp as interpreters over a traced jaxpr.
stuck: Broadcast inputs need their gradient summed back to the input shape; most backward shape errors come from this.
Run backward in reverse topological order, or a node's gradient is read before all contributions arrive.
A node used twice must accumulate its gradient (+=), not overwrite it.
Use float64 for gradient checks; float32 finite differences produce false failures.
If Autodidax Part 4 is hard to follow, finish the dual-number step first.

project.title: Tensor autograd engine that trains a real model, with gradient-checkpointing
project.brief: Extend scalar autograd to a NumPy-backed tensor library with broadcasting, reductions, matmul, softmax and cross-entropy, then train a small MLP or CNN on MNIST to a target accuracy. Add activation checkpointing and measure the memory/compute trade-off; add a forward-mode JVP and use it for a Hessian-vector product.
deliverables: repo with tensor autograd, 20+ ops each with a finite-difference gradient test, and an MNIST training script
README with accuracy curves, peak-memory vs recompute plots for checkpointing, and HVP verification results
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining reverse vs forward mode, broadcasting gradients, and the checkpointing trade-off

rubric.solid: All op gradients pass finite-difference checks (rtol 1e-5 in float64); MNIST MLP reaches 97%+ test accuracy.
rubric.exceptional: Checkpointing cuts peak memory by a measured factor with sqrt(n) segment analysis, HVP via forward-over-reverse verified, and results matched against PyTorch to 1e-6.

title: Deep learning systems
why: Before compiling tensor programs you need a tensor library: strides, broadcasting, autograd on tensors, and fast kernels. MiniTorch and CMU DLSys (10-414/714) build each piece with tests.

steps.detail: 4.1 1D Convolution, 4.2 2D Convolution, 4.3 Pooling, 4.4 Softmax and Dropout, 4.5 Training an Image Classifier (LeNet on MNIST).

steps.title: CMU DLSys Lectures 3-5: Manual Neural Networks / Backprop, Automatic Differentiation, Automatic Differentiation Implementation
steps.detail: Compare needle's computational-graph design with MiniTorch's.

steps.title: DLSys Homework 1: needle autodiff
steps.detail: Implement forward and backward for needle ops and reverse-mode AD with a topological sort (hw1.ipynb).

steps.title: DLSys Lectures 10, 12, 13: Hardware Acceleration for Linear Algebra, Hardware Acceleration + GPUs, Hardware Acceleration Implementation
steps.detail: Focus on the strided NDArray backend design and tiling.

steps.title: DLSys Homework 3: NDArray backend (CPU + CUDA)
steps.detail: Implement compact/setitem, elementwise ops, reductions and tiled matmul in C++ and CUDA (hw3.ipynb).

check: permute/expand/reshape produce views (no data copy) verified by shared storage
All MiniTorch Module 2 tests pass
Your tiled matmul is at least 5x faster than the naive triple loop at 1024x1024
MNIST trains to >97% test accuracy with your library

extra.title: tinygrad source: tensor.py
extra.note: Compare your Tensor API with the real thing.

extra.title: DLSys Homework 4 (CNNs, RNNs)
extra.note: Further model work on your backend.

Implement tensor broadcasting and tensor-level autograd that pass the MiniTorch Module 2 tests.
Write a tiled CPU matmul and a CUDA matmul for an NDArray backend.
Train LeNet on MNIST with your own framework.

Non-contiguous tensors break naive kernels; decide where you call compact()/contiguous() and test both paths.
Softmax and log-softmax overflow unless you subtract the row max.
If training does not learn, overfit a single batch first; failure there means a gradient bug.

project.title: Lazy-evaluating mini-framework with fusion and a benchmark against PyTorch CPU
project.brief: Make your framework lazy: build an op graph, fuse elementwise chains and their following reduction into single generated C kernels, and reuse buffers. Train a 2-layer, 128-dim character-level transformer on Tiny Shakespeare (about 1 MB of text) for 2000 steps and compare speed and memory against your eager mode and PyTorch CPU.
deliverables: repo with lazy graph, fusion pass, codegen backend, memory planner, and a char-level transformer training script
README with kernel-count, peak-memory and tokens/sec comparisons (eager vs fused vs PyTorch CPU) and loss curves
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining the fusion rules, where fusion is illegal, and the memory planner design

rubric.solid: Fused mode launches at least 3x fewer kernels than eager, matches eager outputs to 1e-5, and validation loss falls below 2.0 nats/char.
rubric.exceptional: Within 2x of PyTorch CPU tokens/sec, a liveness-based memory planner with measured savings, and a visualization of the scheduled graph.

title: Performance engineering
why: An ML compiler is only as good as the code it emits. MIT 6.172 covers work, caches, vectorization and measurement; Aalto PPC has you optimize one kernel step by step on CPU, which is what kernel codegen must do automatically.

steps.title: MIT 6.172 Lecture 1: Introduction and Matrix Multiplication
steps.detail: The speedup ladder for matmul: Python, Java, C, loop order, compiler flags, parallel loops, tiling, vectorization.

steps.title: MIT 6.172 Lecture 2: Bentley Rules for Optimizing Work
steps.detail: A catalog of work-reducing transforms; many of them are compiler passes.

steps.title: MIT 6.172 Lecture 4: Assembly Language and Computer Architecture
steps.detail: x86-64 assembly, pipelines and vector units.

steps.title: MIT 6.172 Lecture 5: C to Assembly
steps.detail: How clang lowers C to LLVM IR and then to assembly.

steps.title: MIT 6.172 Lecture 9: What Compilers Can and Cannot Do
steps.detail: What the compiler can prove and what it cannot, including aliasing, inlining and vectorization limits.

steps.title: MIT 6.172 HW2: Profiling Serial Merge Sort and HW3: Vectorization
steps.detail: HW2 uses perf and cachegrind to profile a merge sort. HW3 has you read clang vectorization reports and get loops to vectorize.

steps.title: Aalto PPC Chapter 2: Case study, V0-V7 with the Asm pages
steps.detail: V0 Baseline, V1 Linear reading, V2 Instruction-level parallelism, V3 Vector instructions, V4 Reuse data in registers, V5 More register reuse, V6 Prefetching, V7 Better use of cache memory.

steps.title: Aalto PPC exercises CP1, CP2a, CP2b, CP2c, CP3a
steps.detail: CP1 CPU baseline, CP2a instruction-level parallelism, CP2b multicore parallelism, CP2c vectorization, CP3a fast solution with doubles. Submit to the grader and record runtime per version.

steps.title: Aalto PPC exercise IS4 (image segmentation, fast solution) or MF1 (median filter, CPU baseline)
steps.detail: One more problem with a different access pattern. Optional.

steps.title: Algorithmica HPC: Matrix Multiplication case study
steps.detail: Baseline, transposition, vectorization, register reuse, kernel design, blocking. The author reaches about 50x over naive and BLAS-level speed on a Zen 2 CPU.

steps.title: Hand-optimize a CPU matmul to >50% of peak
steps.detail: In C with intrinsics: naive -> transposed -> blocked -> micro-kernel -> OpenMP; plot GFLOP/s per step.

build: A benchmarked CPU SGEMM in C (callable from your Module 15 library via ctypes) with a writeup plotting GFLOP/s across 6 optimization stages against theoretical peak, plus perf counter evidence (cache misses, IPC) for each stage.
check: You can compute your CPU's theoretical peak FLOP/s from cores, frequency, SIMD width and FMA units
Your final matmul is within 2x of OpenBLAS/numpy at 2048x2048
You can explain from perf counters why loop order i-k-j beats i-j-k
Aalto CP3a passes the grader at the benchmark time limit

How to Optimize a CUDA Matmul Kernel (Simon Boehm)

outcomes: Compute your CPU's theoretical peak FLOP/s and a kernel's arithmetic intensity, and place it on a roofline.
Optimize a CPU SGEMM with blocking, packing, SIMD and threads, and report GFLOP/s per stage.
Use perf (or Instruments on macOS) counters to explain a speedup, such as cache misses dropping after a loop interchange.
Benchmark with warmup, repeated runs, and median plus spread.
stuck: Noisy timings: warm up, repeat, report median and spread; pin threads to cores where possible.
If the compiler removed your benchmark loop, consume the result or use a DoNotOptimize-style barrier.
Check vectorization with -Rpass=loop-vectorize (clang) or -fopt-info-vec (gcc) instead of guessing.
Choose block sizes from your own L1/L2 sizes and measurements.

project.title: CPU SGEMM reaching a stated fraction of peak, with a roofline report
project.brief: Write a single-precision GEMM in C from naive loops to a packed, register-blocked, SIMD (AVX2/AVX-512 or NEON), multithreaded kernel. Document each optimization step with measured GFLOP/s and hardware counters, place each version on a roofline for your machine, and compare to OpenBLAS/Accelerate.
deliverables: repo with each optimization step as a separate tagged version and a reproducible benchmark harness
README with GFLOP/s vs matrix size plots, a roofline chart, and cache-miss counters per version
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining micro-kernel design, packing, and why each step helped

rubric.solid: Single-thread kernel reaches 50%+ of theoretical peak on large sizes; all versions verified against a reference.
rubric.exceptional: 80%+ of peak and within 10–20% of OpenBLAS/Accelerate, with a tuned micro-kernel justified by register/latency arithmetic and multithreaded scaling analysis.

title: Parallelism and GPUs
why: ML compilers target GPUs, so you need the SIMT execution model, the memory hierarchy, and the reasons tiling and fusion matter. CS149 gives the model, GPU Puzzles drills indexing, and real CUDA kernels prepare you to emit them.

steps.title: Stanford CS149 slides, Lectures 1-3: Why Parallelism? Why Efficiency?, A Modern Multi-Core Processor, Multi-Core Architecture Part II + ISPC
steps.detail: Multi-core, SIMD, hardware multithreading, latency vs bandwidth. The page at this URL is labeled the Fall 2022 offering.

steps.title: CS149 Assignment 1: Programs 1-6 (fractal with threads, SIMD intrinsics, ISPC, sqrt, saxpy, k-means)
steps.detail: Program 1 threads, 2 SIMD intrinsics, 3 ISPC (including tasks), 4 iterative sqrt, 5 BLAS saxpy, 6 k-means. Write the analysis each program asks for.

steps.title: CS149 slides, Lecture 7: GPU Architecture and CUDA Programming
steps.detail: CUDA abstractions and how they map to hardware: threads, blocks, warps, shared memory.

steps.title: GPU Puzzles 1-14 (Map, Zip, Guards, Map 2D, Broadcast, Blocks, Blocks 2D, Shared, Pooling, Dot Product, 1D Convolution, Prefix Sum, Axis Sum, Matrix Multiply)
steps.detail: Run in Colab with Numba's CUDA simulator. Puzzles 1-14.

steps.detail: Part 1 SAXPY, Part 2 exclusive prefix sum and find_repeats, Part 3 circle renderer (85 of 100 points).

steps.detail: Read the programming model, then the SIMT kernel chapter for memory spaces, shared memory and coalescing.

steps.title: How to Optimize a CUDA Matmul Kernel (Simon Boehm): kernels 1-6
steps.detail: Reproduce Kernel 1 naive, 2 global memory coalescing, 3 shared memory cache-blocking, 4 1D blocktiling, 5 2D blocktiling, 6 vectorized SMEM and GMEM access. Compare each against cuBLAS.

steps.title: Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr From First Principles (Horace He)
steps.detail: Compute, memory-bandwidth and overhead as the three costs, and why fusing memory-bound ops helps.

steps.title: Generate CUDA from your IR
steps.detail: Read tinygrad's C-style renderer, then emit CUDA source from your rewrite-IR for elementwise and reduce kernels, compile with NVRTC or nvcc, and run.

build: A CUDA backend for your tensor library: hand-written tiled SGEMM reaching >50% of cuBLAS, plus a code generator that turns fused elementwise+reduce graphs from your IR into CUDA kernels, validated against numpy and benchmarked against unfused execution.
check: All 14 GPU Puzzles pass

Your matmul reports achieved memory bandwidth and FLOP/s and you can say which bound applies
A fused kernel for relu(x*w+b).sum() is faster than three separate kernels

outcomes: Write CUDA kernels with correct thread, block and warp indexing and bounds guards.
Optimize a GPU SGEMM through coalescing, shared-memory tiling, register blocktiling and vectorized loads.
Use Nsight Compute to state whether a kernel is memory-bound or compute-bound, with numbers.
Implement a parallel exclusive scan and a numerically stable softmax on the GPU.
stuck: Uncoalesced global loads are the most common slowdown; check the per-warp access pattern, then confirm in Nsight Compute's memory section.
A missing __syncthreads() gives intermittently wrong results; run compute-sanitizer --tool racecheck.
Shared-memory bank conflicts: pad the tile (for example 32x33) and measure.
Higher occupancy is not always faster; register tiling often wins at lower occupancy.
No NVIDIA GPU: GPU Puzzles run in Colab; for asst3 and SGEMM use a cloud or Colab GPU.
